summary: Defines MIB objects, in SMIv2 format, for managing the configuration, monitoring and control of SNA data link controls using SNMP. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: Gauges for watching connections of an old IBM networking system.

questions: how to manage sdlc with snmp
subtitle: SNMP management of IBM's SNA data link control connections

tldr.problem: IBM's SNA network environments had SDLC (Synchronous Data Link Control) ports and logical link connections that needed to be configured, monitored, and managed through standard network management tools.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1747 defines a set of MIB objects in SMIv2 format organized into six tables: three for ports (administrative, operational, and statistics) and three for link stations (administrative, operational, and statistics).
tldr.outcome: The RFC enabled SNMP-based management of legacy SNA/SDLC equipment, but is now historic as SNA and SDLC are obsolete technologies.

today: RFC 1747 is now historic. SDLC and SNA are obsolete technologies. Modern networks use IP-based protocols instead of SNA for enterprise networking.

sections.title: Overview of SDLC Management
sections.content:
The SNMPv2 Network Management Framework allows network administrators to configure, monitor, and control network devices. RFC 1747 extends this framework to cover Synchronous Data Link Control (SDLC), which is IBM's protocol for managing connections in SNA networks. SDLC operates at the data link layer (layer 2) and is responsible for the reliable transmission of data over a link.

The MIB defines managed objects for two distinct types of entities in SDLC: ports (the physical connections) and link stations (the logical connections that operate over a port). Each entity has three categories of management tables: administrative tables for configuration and control, operational tables reflecting the current state, and statistics tables measuring performance and errors.
sections.eli5: IBM's old SNA networks had real cables (ports) and virtual connections (link stations). This memo says how to see and change what they are doing using standard network management tools.

sections.title: Port and Link Station Structure
sections.content:
SDLC ports are the physical communication interfaces, such as RS-232, V.35, or other serial line connections. Each port can operate in either point-to-point mode (connecting to one other station) or multipoint mode (connecting to multiple other stations). A port can be configured as a primary station (issuing commands to secondary stations) or a secondary station (responding to a primary), or negotiable (able to assume either role).

Link stations are the logical connections that operate over a port. In multipoint topologies, a single port can have multiple link stations, each with a unique poll address. In point-to-point topologies, there is typically one link station per port. The administrative tables allow configuration of these entities, while operational tables show their current state (active, inactive, pending), and statistics tables track counters for frames transmitted and received, errors, and other metrics.
sections.eli5: A port is the actual wire. A link station is a connection through that wire. One port can have many link stations if it talks to many devices.

sections.title: Administrative Configuration
sections.content:
The administrative tables allow network administrators to configure SDLC behavior. Port administrative objects include the port name, the role it plays (primary or secondary), whether it connects to a leased or switched line, the topology (point-to-point or multipoint), and timing parameters such as activity timeouts and poll pause intervals. These parameters control how the port behaves when it is started and can be changed while the port is running, though some changes only take effect after the port is cycled inactive.

Link station administrative objects control the configuration of individual logical connections, such as the remote station address (poll address), modulo (the number of outstanding frames that can be unacknowledged), retry limits, and timeouts. Row status objects allow administrators to create new link stations and remove existing ones using SNMP set operations.
sections.eli5: Administrative tables let you say: this port is primary, talks to a leased line, uses point-to-point, and polls every 100 milliseconds. For link stations you set the address, retry count, and timeouts.

sections.title: Operational State and Status
sections.content:
The operational tables report the current state of SDLC ports and link stations. Port operational objects show whether the port is currently active or inactive, the actual baud rate, the current number of active link stations, and the recent activity level. Link station operational objects report the state of each connection: inactive, pending (trying to establish), active (successfully established), or other states. These read-only objects reflect the real-time condition of the port and its link stations, which may differ from the administrative configuration if a configuration change has not yet taken effect or if equipment failure has occurred.

The operational tables integrate with the standard interfaces group of MIB-II by reporting through the ifTable with ifType value 17 (SDLC). Each SDLC port appears as an interface entry, and the relationship between the SDLC layer and its underlying physical layer (RS-232, V.35, etc.) is modeled using the ifStackTable.
sections.eli5: Operational tables show what is actually happening right now: this port is running, that link station is active, the line speed is 9600 baud. These are read-only because they reflect reality, not wishes.

sections.title: Performance Counters and Statistics
sections.content:
The statistics tables maintain counters and metrics for SDLC performance monitoring. Port statistics include counts of frames transmitted and received, bytes sent and received, various error categories (frame errors, CRC errors, timeouts), and counters for aborts and resets. Link station statistics track frames and bytes for each connection, plus error counters specific to that link station such as retry timeouts, secondary transmit underruns, and command/response synchronization errors.

These counters allow network administrators and automated management systems to detect problems: high error rates might indicate a noisy line, increasing timeout counters might suggest network congestion or a hung device, and low activity might indicate a disconnected station. The RFC integrates these link-layer counters with the standard ifTable and ifStackTable interfaces so that management applications can correlate SDLC statistics with other network statistics.
sections.eli5: Statistics tables count frames sent, frames received, and all the ways they can fail: bad checksums, timeouts, retries, and resets. Managers watch these numbers to see if the network is healthy.

sections.title: Standards Compliance and Conformance
sections.content:
RFC 1747 defines conformance groups and compliance statements to specify which objects an SNMP agent must implement to claim conformance to the SDLC MIB. The specification requires implementation of the ifGeneralGroup, ifStackGroup, and ifPacketGroup from the standard interfaces group, ensuring that SDLC ports integrate cleanly with the standard management framework. Optional implementation of the ifTestGroup allows vendors to define and expose proprietary diagnostic tests, such as link pulse detection and analysis (LPDA) functions.

The RFC also specifies the relationship between SDLC management and higher-layer SNA entities: while this MIB covers only SDLC ports and link stations, the management of Physical Units (PU) and Logical Units (LU) in SNA is handled by the separate SNA NAU (Network Addressable Unit) MIB. This separation allows each layer of the network to be managed through its own specialized MIB.
sections.eli5: The RFC says: if you want to manage SDLC with SNMP, you must support these base tables and can optionally support vendor-specific tests. You use this MIB for the link layer and another MIB for what runs on top.
